transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-21
Time: 16:00 UTC (8:00 PT)
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Anya (CTO, Crucible AI), Marcus (ML Eng), Priya (Head of Infra), Ben (Product)

--- Optional auto-generated summary (AI):
Customer evaluating Redwood for low-latency streaming inference. Primary success criteria: p95 <= 200ms for short-turn streaming endpoints, support for high concurrency bursts (hundreds to ~1k concurrent streams), predictable cost, and enterprise controls (SSO, KMS, audit logs).

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intro from our side — I’m Maya, AE on the Redwood platform, and this is Diego, our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Anya: Good, thanks. We wanted to focus on your streaming behavior and p95, cause our product is real-time chat. We have some SLOs we can't break.
[00:12] Marcus: Yeah hi — Marcus here. We did some internal prototyping with a few open models, but the latency's all over the place when concurrency spikes.
[00:20] Priya: And from infra, we care about consistent cold start behavior and also KV cache locality, we run on k8s with node pools of A100s.
[00:27] Diego: Great, can I start with a quick set of questions about your traffic profile? Typical turn length, tokens per second, and burst characteristics?
[00:34] Ben: Typical user messages are 8-24 tokens, but replies are 40-150 tokens. We do a lot of short-turn flows. Average session has 6-10 turns.
[00:43] Anya: Important: p95 must be under 200ms for the initial stream token arrival to the client for short replies — that's our internal SLO for perceived interactivity.
[00:52] Diego: Understood. Just so I set expectations, p95 for streaming depends on network, inference time per token, batching strategy and KV cache hits. Hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs are often about predictable capacity and warm pools.
[01:04] Marcus: We run a couple models — 13B and a custom 30B finetune. Which models does Redwood host? Any verified perf profiles for these sizes?
[01:13] Maya: Redwood has a model catalog, we publish performance profiles; for finetunes we usually test locally, but we can run baseline benchmarking. Diego, maybe mention the quantized path?
[01:20] Diego: Sure. We support int8 / 4-bit quantized variants on our runtime; quantization reduces memory and often reduces token inference time, but results vary by model. For streaming the KV cache behavior and prefix caching matter a lot. If your workload has high cache hit rate you'll see big wins.
[01:36] Speaker 1: (inaudible) quanization spelled weird in notes
[01:40] Priya: About hosting options: we're evaluating Hosted for speed to market, Dedicated reserved pools for predictability, and Private (VPC) for compliance. What's the difference in cold-starts?
[01:50] Diego: Hosted: quickest onboarding, but cold-starts can be slightly more variable unless you provision reserved capacity or use warmup policies. Dedicated: you get your own GPU pool, much more stable p95 and predictable throttling. Private: same runtime in your VPC, but extra ops overhead for deployment and KMS integration.
[02:05] Anya: We need to know how fallback works — for example, if the main pool is saturated, do requests route to lower-cost models and what does that do to latency?
[02:12] Diego: We have smart routing policies. We can fallback to a compatible lower-capacity model; the key is ensuring semantic acceptability. Fallbacks are instant but will change output characteristics and cost. For latency alone, smaller models are faster.
[02:22] Marcus: Concrete numbers: For a 30B finetune, what p95 can we expect per token on an A100-ish class node with no batching?
[02:31] Diego: Ballpark: unbatched single-token latency for a 30B with int8 might be ~30-40ms per token on optimized runtimes, so for a 50-token reply that's ~1.5-2s if fully sequential. But with streaming the client gets tokens as generated; your p95 for first few tokens is dominated by context prep and kv warmup. With batching and proper caching we can drive token/sec throughput far higher.
[02:51] Priya: That seems high. Our product expects first token under 200ms. Are there configuration levers — smaller model, quantization, or pinned reserved pools?
[02:59] Diego: Yes. Options: 1) use a smaller specialized model for short replies, 2) enable aggressive prefix/KV caching so generation starts from warmed KV, 3) reserved dedicated capacity to eliminate noisy neighbors and cold starts, and 4) adjust microbatching thresholds to trade latency for throughput.
[03:18] Anya: Tell us about streaming benchmarks — what do you run and what do you need from us?
[03:23] Maya: We usually run a representative trace with your prompt distribution, token lengths, and concurrency mix. Diego will share a script that replays traffic at token-level granularity and measures p50/p95/p99.
[03:33] Diego: We'll need sample prompt traces (anonymized) and ideally an S3 bucket where you put the KV warm prefixes. For private workloads we can test on our hosted cluster with customer data redacted, or run the pilot in a dedicated reserved pool.
[03:47] Ben: About KV cache locality — our turn lengths mean prefixes overlap a lot, so cache hit rate should be high. How does Redwood manage prefix cache across nodes?
[03:56] Diego: We do automatic prefix/KV caching and attempt to colocate hot keys. In Dedicated/Private you can get better locality because we control routing to keep affinity. In Hosted, we also try to keep affinity but ISPs may route you differently; it's more probabilistic unless you pin routes.
[04:11] Marcus: Anything around steady-state throughput? We may have bursts of up to 800 concurrent short streams lasting a couple minutes.
[04:19] Diego: For bursts we recommend sizing for 1) sustained baseline + 2) burst capacity via autoscaling policies and burst pools. For example, a reserved pool sized for 400 steady concurrent streams with autoscale headroom can absorb spikes to 800 if burst capacity is enabled, though that increases cost during spikes.
[04:35] Priya: On security: SSO, SAML, SOC2, audit logs, and KMS — can Redwood integrate with our enterprise KMS and give per-request encryption logs?
[04:44] Maya: Yes. Private deployments support customer-managed KMS/HSM and full audit logs. Hosted supports KMS integration and audit trails, but enterprise contracts are needed for dedicated retention windows. We'll send the SOC2 and architecture docs.
[04:56] Anya: One blocker: we need deterministic p95 at peak. If hosting variability is too high, we'll need Private. Can you estimate variance?
[05:04] Diego: With Dedicated pools and pinned routing variance is low — within ~5-10% p95 drift in our tests. Hosted general-purpose clusters can see higher variance during noisy neighbor events unless you provision reserved capacity or dedicated lanes.
[05:18] Marcus: Let's talk about a pilot. We want to validate p95 for 30B finetune on our prompts with concurrency up to 500, streaming first token under 200ms for majority. What's a realistic pilot setup?
[05:29] Maya: We propose a 2-week pilot: week 1 onboarding and small-scale validation on hosted dedicated pool (reserved capacity), week 2 scale up to target concurrency with burst tests. Redwood provides benchmark scripts, and we'll coordinate a security checklist.
[05:41] Diego: For the benchmarks we'll run: cold-start profile, warm-run p50/p95/p99, KV cache hit/miss scenarios, and a token/sec sustained run to measure throughput and GPU utilization. We'll include both quantized and fp16 variants.
[05:58] Priya: Cost attention: we need an estimate of cost per 1M tokens at your recommended config, and delta vs smaller model.
[06:06] Maya: We'll include cost modelling in the worksheet, with cost-per-token and cost-per-session. Also show how batching/caching reduces unit cost.
[06:13] Ben: Any limitations in terms of model size we can't host?
[06:17] Diego: We support up to large model variants; for very large (>70B) we recommend model parallel or sharded deployments which we can discuss. For your 30B it's straightforward.
[06:26] Anya: Questions from our infra: how is KV cache persisted across restarts? Will a node reboot lose warmed KV and spike p95?
[06:33] Diego: Warm caches are in-memory for hot performance; we also have an optional persistent prefix store that allows faster rebuilds after restarts. That reduces cold-start spike. We'll demo that in the pilot.
[06:46] Marcus: For the tracer — do you support per-token tracing and token timestamps in logs?
[06:51] Diego: Yes; we emit token-level timing and request traces in the Console with token timestamps and route-level breakdown (network, scheduling, inference).
[06:58] Anya: Ok, sounds reasonable. Let's recap next steps.
[07:02] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send pilot worksheet, Diego to send scripts + perf checklist, customer to share traces and infra notes, schedule pilot kickoff. We'll also send SOC2 and security docs.
[07:12] Priya: We'll try to get the traces by Wednesday and confirm kickoff time.
[07:15] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with all artifacts.

[End of call — recording stops]

Notes/observations (auto): occasional ASR mistakes ("quanization" for quantization), speaker attribution sometimes generic. Conversation balanced between AE qualification and SE technical depth. Emphasis on p95 streaming and cache-locality, pilot agreement in principle.
